title: Two agents, same prompt, one had a RAG library of game-dev books
author: zjgkkn
selftext:
Two Claude Opus 5.5 agents built a Unity game from the same idea: a top-down descent

down an endless well, dark-fantasy mood. Same tools, all assets from local models.



The only difference: one agent had a RAG library (vector DB) of game-dev books, and it

used it actively, with 32 searches and 7 passage reads. Its design doc cites a book and

page for each system (Game Feel, Game Balance, PCG in Games…). The other had none.

  
In the video: Ashwell first (with RAG), then Lanternfall (no RAG).

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: Cool experiment but I'm not sure what to look for.

replies.author: zjgkkn
replies.body:
I don’t have any professional experience in game development; I’m currently putting together a toolkit to turn this into a hobby.

The goal of this post was to figure out whether providing AI agents with game development books as part of their context is a standard practice -- and whether it’s something that should always be done by default. Based on my experiment, I’m leaning toward "yes" -- it is worth doing.

I am taking the opportunity to get comments from users who have more experience.

Thanks!

replies.author: zjgkkn
replies.body:
My conclusion as of now: "Dumb" models rely heavily on learned patterns. Additional materials -- such as book chapters --require a level of understanding that these models simply lack; in fact, feeding them books often does more harm than good.

Smarter models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, are capable of utilizing RAG without any noticeable drop in quality. However, the actual benefit remains unclear to me -- perhaps more experience is needed. So far, my experiments have been limited to prompts like "Claude, make a game," which clearly doesn't align with the intended use case for such a model.

replies.author: zjgkkn
replies.body:
Yep. Here is the examples of queries produced by agent:

\- risk and reward choices in core gameplay loop, meaningful decisions

\- falling damage proportional to height, punishment for mistakes, player failure feedback

\- parallax scrolling layers create illusion of depth

\- air control while jumping and falling, gravity, how much to steer in midair

\- endless runner procedural level generation chunks, guaranteeing playability, reachable platforms

\- enemy attack telegraphing, anticipation before attack so the player can react

\- ambient sound loops and interactive music layers that change with tension or player health

  
He received some kind of result almost instantly; in the context of the internet, this might have required a fairly in-depth investigation.

replies.author: zjgkkn
replies.body:
Both agents developed nearly identical mechanics: jumping (no double jump), movement, and one attack animation. In the version without RAG, there were three types of enemies, compared to two in the version with RAG -- though I suspect this is more likely due to the seed than RAG.

https://i.redd.it/hgbjngk4710i1.png

I also conducted a similar experiment using DeepSeek, and the results were vastly different; the agent utilizing RAG failed to assemble a level without significant defects.

comments.author: SomeoneGMForMe
comments.body:
AI's sure do love lanterns, embers, crowns, and all of those things falling.

I'd recommend adding a prompt before starting any project that's something like "research what concepts and words are more likely to appear in ai generated fiction and create a list of "slop", and then any time you generate lore concepts, titles, and other strings, check them against the slop list".  Ghosts and lighthouses are some other common concepts that AI goes to again and again in fiction.

It works fairly well; there are some good published papers on words and concepts which appear more frequently in AI generated writing than in human generated writing which Claude can find and read.

Note that I'm using slop here as a technical term to mean any content generated by AI that looks too AI-ish or uncannily nonhuman, and Claude will happily recognize that term and review its own output based on it.

comments.author: CodeGuyJay
comments.body:
I couldn't really tell the difference between the two to be honest.

To be honest I don't really understand how RAG is helpful here. Usually RAG is used to hydrate a model with knowledge that it wasn't trained on. 

In this case, how does the model know when it should consult the knowledge base vs just try to solve the problem on its own? Does it now consult the knowledge base for every single possible query you ask for? Seems counterproductive.

replies.author: zjgkkn
replies.body:
Key differences in the design documents (game design docs) generated by the two agents:

\- In the version without RAG the environment exerts constant pressure on the player; there is a mechanic involving a depleting bar that must be replenished. In the version with RAG, the game structure follows a pattern of "segment - ​​respite - segment."

\- With RAG, the player can always see where they will land; platforms are highlighted and visible in advance. Without RAG, the agent arrived at a mechanic where platforms only appear as the player approaches. The agent found a reference in the source material stating: "the player should always be able to see where they will land."

\- Visual communication: With RAG, the lantern (an essential element) dims in proportion to the player's health. Only safe platforms those that won't break are marked in blue. A "danger metric" determines the audio loop.

In this instance, I explicitly instructed the agent to actively utilize RAG while implementing each game component. Without this directive, the agent would only make queries during the initial design document creation phase, and even then, it would do so reluctantly.

replies.author: zjgkkn
replies.body:
\> Usually RAG is used to hydrate a model with knowledge that it wasn't trained on.  
  
Not really. The size of a model is smaller than the dataset it is trained on, even when compressed. This means that the data -- even if the model has "seen" it can still have an effect.
